Abstract 
What if you could try on an outfit without leaving your screen? Online shoppers still guess their size, guess which 
pieces go together  and guess how a garment will look on them, and wrong guesses end in returns and lost 
confidence. FitStyle AI answers these guesses in one shopping workflow. From a single full-body photograph and 
her height, a body -measurement model estimates shoulder, wa ist and hip widths, a body shape and a clothing 
size. An outfit-recommendation engine then proposes five complete outfits for her size, body shape, occasion and 
season, offers only items that are in stock in her size, and explains each choice in plain language. The shopper can 
swap any piece, preview the look on her own photograph with the LaDI -VTON virtual try-on model, build a cart,

the LaDI -VTON virtual try-on model, build a cart, 
and reserve or pay for it. The web application runs locally, its database and authentication use cloud services 
within free -tier limits, and the try -on model runs as a service on a free GPU notebook runtime. The 
recommendation engine, the most data -driven component, was evaluated against catalogue -derived labels: a 
rebalanced compatibility model reached 0.789 held-out accuracy, up from 0.646, and a per-item reuse cap raised 
the number of distinct items in the top five outfits from 8 to 14. For body measurement, replacing landmark 
distances with silhouette widths corrected an implausible hip estimate on a test photograph. The try -on model 
was assessed only qualitatively, and generating an outfit takes minutes on a free GPU. No u

rating an outfit takes minutes on a free GPU. No user study was 
conducted, so claims about shopper preference remain open. The project shows that measurement, 
recommendation and preview can be combined in one low-cost application.

1. Introduction 
1.1 Background 
Online fashion retail lets shoppers browse thousands of products from home, but it lacks two things that a physical 
fitting room provides: confirmation that a garment will fit the wearer, and the chance to see how pieces look 
together on her. Han et al. observe that the ubiquity of online fashion shopping demands effective 
recommendation services for customers [4]. Fit is a commercial as well as a personal problem: Sheikh et al. note 
that predicting the correct fit improves customer satisfaction and reduces the cost of size -related returns [13]. 
Style is a second source of uncertainty: Koukopoulos et al. argue that outfit recommendat ions simplify decision-
making, increase consumer confidence and raise conversion rates [7]. At the same time, advan

aise conversion rates [7]. At the same time, advances in computer 
vision, vision–language models and managed cloud services make it feasible to offer these capabilities inside an 
ordinary web shop. 
1.2 Problem Statement 
A shopper who buys clothes online faces three connected problems. (i) Size uncertainty: size charts differ between 
brands and shoppers rarely know their own measurements, so they order several sizes or return items. (ii) Outfit 
uncertainty: shops usually present products one by one, leaving the shopper to decide which garments go 
together for a given occasion and body shape. (iii) Lack of preview: the shopper cannot see a garment on herself 
before buying. These problems are norm ally handled by separate tools, if at all, so the shopper must combine 
several sources

all, so the shopper must combine 
several sources of advice by herself. The problem addressed by this project is how to bring measurement, 
recommendation and preview together in one low-cost shopping application whose database and authentication 
use cloud services. 
1.3 Motivation 
A single workflow that starts from one photograph can remove manual steps for the shopper and give the shop 
fewer wrong -size purchases and a more engaging experience. The project is also motivat ed by a practical 
engineering question: whether a complete application with three AI components, user accounts, a product 
catalogue, a cart, checkout and administrator tools can be built by a small team using the free tiers of managed 
cloud services for data, authentication and storage, with the cloud resources de

ntication and storage, with the cloud resources defined as code so that they can be 
reproduced. 
1.4 Project Overview 
FitStyle AI  is an AI -powered fashion fitting platform with cloud computing. The shopper creates an account, 
uploads a full-body photograph, reviews the body measurements and clothing size that the system infers, chooses 
an occasion, receives recommended outfits, previews garments on her photograph, and adds the selected items 
to a cart and pays. Administrators manage the product catalogue and view sales analytics. The front end is a React 
single-page application and the back end is a Node.js/Express server; both run locally on the team’s machine and 
are not hosted in the cloud. The cloud is used for identity and data only: authentication uses Amazon Cognito, the

The objectives of the project are as follows. 
• O1. Platform. To build a secure web application, whose data and authentication are handled by cloud 
services, with user accounts, a product catalogue, a shopping cart, checkout and order history, and 
administrator tools for product management and sales analytics. 
• O2. Body measurement and size. To estimate body measurements, body shape and clothing size from a

• O3. Outfit recommendation. To recommend complete outfits that suit the shopper’s size, body shape, 
occasion and season, using only products that are in stock in her size, and to explain each recommendation 
(Model 2). 
• O4. Virtual try-on. To let the shopper preview a selected garment on her own photograph (Model 3). 
• O5. Integration. To connect the three models and the platform into one workflow in which the output of

• O6. Low cost and reproducibility.  To design the system so that the cloud services it uses (a database,

1.6 Research Questions 
The project addresses four research questions. RQ1: how accurately can body me asurements, a body shape and 
a clothing size be inferred from a single photograph and the shopper’s stated height? RQ2: can a catalogue -
grounded recommendation engine compose complete outfits that suit a shopper’s size, body shape, occasion and

compatibility model add over simple baselines when its labels are derived from catalogue attributes? RQ4: can a 
commerce platform and three AI component s be integrated using only the free tiers of cloud services for data, 
authentication and storage? 
1.7 Scope and Limitations 
The project covers the full shopper journey from photograph to payment for a single shop with a catalogue of 
11,513 products drawn from a public dataset [14]. The catalogue stocks sizes S to XL only. The AI components are

by the recommendation engine are derived from catal ogue att

simulated for the purposes of the project. The body -measurement model uses a single front -facing photograph 
and a stated height, and its behaviour has so far been examined on a few photographs without tape -measure 
ground truth (Section 5.2).

2. Background and Literature Review 
2.1 Size and Fit in Online Fashion 
Fit is a central source of friction in online fashio n. Sheikh et al. propose a deep -learning, content-collaborative 
approach to personalised size and fit recommendation and report that it improves over previously published 
results on two public datasets [13]. Such systems infer fit from purchase history and article data. FitStyle AI instead 
estimates body measurements directly from a photograph, so that a shopper with no purchase history can still 
receive a size. 
Estimating body measurements from a single photograph combines three sub -problems: locating the body, 
delimiting its contour, and recovering absolute scale. For locating the body, BlazePose is a lightweight 
convolutional network that infers 33 b

ightweight 
convolutional network that infers 33 body keypoints and was designed for real-time inference on mobile devices 
[16]. The MediaPipe Pose Landmarke r used in this project follows the same 33 -landmark scheme, returns 
landmarks in image and in world coordinates, and can optionally return a segmentation mask that gives, for each 
pixel, the likelihood of belonging to the detected person [22]. The distinct ion between the two outputs matters 
for clothing measurements: landmarks such as the hips mark internal joint centres, not the external contour on 
which garments are sized, so a distance between landmarks is not a body width. A segmentation mask, in contrast, 
can be read at any height and therefore gives widths at the shoulders, chest, waist, hips and thigh. 
A single image h

s, chest, waist, hips and thigh. 
A single image has no absolute scale. Günel et al. note that recovering a person’s height from one image is 
important for virtual garment fitting but i nherently ambiguous without camera information, and report as their 
central finding that height can only be estimated with large uncertainty [21]. FitStyle AI therefore does not infer 
the shopper’s height; it asks for it and uses it as the reference length. 
The measurement module started from a landmark-based baseline in which each body dimension is computed as 
the Euclidean distance between two landmarks and converted to centimetres with a factor derived from the 
person’s known height. Section 3.2 describes two limitations of this baseline that were found experimentally and 
the corrections that were

Learning-based methods estimate body measurements directly. Ruiz et al. train a Body Measurement network on 
silhouette images of real subjects, augment its training data with an adversarial body simulator built on a

measurements derived from 3D scans; their setting constrains the pos

This method needs training data and two views; the geometric approach of this project needs no training data 
and a single view, at the price of the limitations discussed in Section 6.7. 
Body-shape classification is a separate problem. The Female Figure Identification Technique (FFIT) distinguishes 
nine shapes (hourglass, bottom hourglass, top hourglass, spoon, rectangle, diamond, oval, triangle and inverted 
triangle) from girth measurements, which is an advance on earlier classifications based on 2D widths [24]. Parker 
et al. show, however, that slight differences in the definition of the measurements can place the same body in 
different FFIT shapes in up to 40% of cases, and that FFIT omi

garment construction [24]. The definitions themselves are standardised in ISO 8559 -1, which describes the 
anthropometric measurements used for clothing, for example the hip as a horizontal girth at the greatest 
projection of the buttocks [24], [25]. Two consequences follow for this project: a width read from a front -facing 
silhouette is not a standard clothing measurement, and a body-shape label obtained from it should be treated as 
approximate. 
2.2 Vision–Language Representations for Fashion 
Contrastive language–image pre-training (CLIP) learns a joint embedding space for images and text from a very 
large collection of image–text pairs and enables zero-shot transfer to new tasks by referring to visual concepts in 
natural language [1]. Chia et al. adapted this idea to retail

uage [1]. Chia et al. adapted this idea to retail with FashionCLIP, a CLIP-like model trained on a fashion 
catalogue, and released its weights [2], [15]. The present system uses Marqo -FashionCLIP, a fashion -domain 
model fine -tuned from a ViT -B-16 CLIP checkpoint using Generalised Contrastive Learning, which trains on 
categories, styles, colours and materials in addition to product descriptions [3]. Its embeddings are used here 
frozen, and natural -language prompts about occasion and silhouette a re embedded in the same space as the 
product images. This is a different checkpoint from the one described by Chia et al.; the two are related by 
approach rather than identical. 
2.3 Outfit Compatibility Learning 
Han et al. formulated outfit compatibility a s a sequence -modelling proble

fit compatibility a s a sequence -modelling problem, treating an outfit as an ordered 
sequence of items and training a bidirectional LSTM jointly with a visual–semantic embedding on a newly collected 
Polyvore dataset [4]. Vasileva et al. showed that learning image embeddings t hat respect item type improves 
outfit-compatibility prediction and fill-in-the-blank tasks over the state of the art at the time [5]. More recently, 
Kalashi and Teimourpour propose a hybrid framework that introduces an “outfit token” to represent the globa l 
context of an outfit and addresses compatibility prediction and complementary-item retrieval together [6]. These 
works rely on large outfit corpora with human-curated positive outfits. FitStyle AI has no such corpus; it therefore 
learns a pairwise compatib

h corpus; it therefore 
learns a pairwise compatibility function from catalogue-derived labels and incorporates item category explicitly, 
in the spirit of type-aware modelling [5]. 
2.4 Outfit Recommendation Systems in Practice 
TrendGen is an outfit recommendation and display system deployed on a major e-commerce platform; it extracts 
product attributes from images and titles and ranks products by aesthetic similarity as well as repetitiveness, so 
that generated outfits are cohesive and varied [7]. Loom combines slot -constrained nearest-neighbour retrieval 
over FashionCLIP embeddings with a multi -objective score covering embedding similarity, colour harmony, 
formality, occasion coherence, style direction and within-outfit diversity, and introduces “vibe/anti-vibe” occasion 
priors

and introduces “vibe/anti-vibe” occasion 
priors that embed prose descripti ons of an occasion as anchor vectors in CLIP space [8]. The occasion -affinity 
component of the present engine follows the same general idea: an occasion is represented by a descriptive 
prompt and by a contrasting prompt, and products are scored by their differential similarity to the two. 
2.5 Model Combination, Branch Balance and Diversity 
Cheng et al. introduced Wide & Deep learning, which jointly trains a linear model and a deep network to combine 
the memorisation of feature interactions with the generali sation of embeddings [9]. Meng et al. study branch

13 
imbalance in dual -branch multimodal networks and show that an imbalance between branches degrades 
downstream performance [10]; this motivated the rebalancing of the visual and metadata branches of the 
compatibility network used here (Section 5.3). For constructing sets of results, Vijayakumar et al. show that 
standard beam search tends to return sequences that differ only slightly, and propose Diverse Beam Search, which 
optimises a diversity -augmented objective [11]. The present engine addresses the analogous problem at outfit 
level with a per-item reuse cap. 
2.6 Sensitivity of Weighted-Sum Rankings 
Outfit scores in this work are weighted sums of relevance and compatibility. O’Shea et al. develop a closed -form 
method for computing weight stability intervals for the weighted

uting weight stability intervals for the weighted sum model, that is, the range of a criterion 
weight over which the ranking of alternatives does not change [12]. Following this principle, the sensitivity of the 
recommended outfit set to its weights is measured and reported (Section 5.3.5) rather than assumed. 
2.7 Virtual Try-On 
Image-based virtual try-on synthesises an image of a person wearing a garment that is shown on its own, or on 
another model, in a product photograph. Early methods  such as VITON predict a coarse try -on image from a 
person representation and the clothing item and then refine it [18]. Progress was limited by data: public datasets 
concentrated on upper-body garments at low resolution. Dress Code addressed this with 53, 795 image pairs at 
1024 × 768 pixels in

with 53, 795 image pairs at 
1024 × 768 pixels in three categories, upper body, lower body and dresses [26], which are the garment categories 
of a fashion shop. 
Recent work builds on diffusion models. Latent diffusion models generate images in the compressed latent space 
of an autoencoder instead of pixel space [27], which makes high -resolution synthesis affordable, and their 
inpainting variants complete a masked region of an image under a condition. IDM-VTON adds garment-encoding 
modules to a diffusion model so that the details of the garment are preserved in unconstrained photographs [19]. 
LaDI-VTON, the model used in this work, treats try-on as latent-diffusion inpainting of the clothing region and adds 
two components [20]: an additional autoencoder module with learnable skip c

dditional autoencoder module with learnable skip connections, which helps to preserve 
the characteristics of the person, and a textual -inversion component, which maps the visual features of the 
garment into the CLIP token -embedding space as pseudo -word embeddings that condition the generation . Its 
authors report that it outperforms competing methods on the Dress Code and VITON-HD datasets by a consistent 
margin [20]. 
LaDI-VTON was chosen as Model 3 for three reasons. Its code and trained weights are public [28], so it can be run 
without a per-call quota or the availability of an external provider. Its Dress Code weights cover tops, bottoms and 
dresses, the categories on which the shop’s catalogue and Model 2 operate. And it needs only the garment image 
as a condition, so no tex

3. Methodology 
3.1 Overall Pipeline 
A shopper’s journey through FitStyle AI has four stages. (1) The shopper uploads a full-body photograph. (2) Model 
1 estimates body measurements, a body shape and a clothing size. (3) The shopper selects an occasion, and Model 
2 returns five complete outfits for the resulting profile (size, body shape, occasion, season). (4) The shopper selects 
an outfit, may replace individual garments, and previews the selected garments on her photograph with Model 3 
(LaDI-VTON). The interface between the models is therefore a small, discrete profile: Model 1 supplies body shape 
and size, and Model 2 consumes them together with the occasion and season (Figure 3.1, in which the shaded

3.2.1 Design rationale and overview 
The module was developed from a landmark-based baseline and improved through two experimental diagnoses. 
The first concerned hip width: the distance between the two hip l andmarks does not measure the width of the 
hips as worn, because those landmarks mark joint centres (Section 5.2). The second concerned the waist: a 
segmentation-based search for the narrowest point of the torso is correct for fitted clothing but fails for loose or 
untucked garments (Section 5.2). The final pipeline, called detect_size(), keeps the landmark distance only where

the waist estimate with a plausibility check, and reports how each waist value was obtained. Figure 3.2

The recommendation experiments support three conclusions. First, rebalancing  the compatibility network 
improved held-out accuracy from 0.646 to 0.789. Second, the per -item reuse cap increased outfit -set diversity 
with negligible relevance cost. Third, the end -to-end evaluation exposed a candidate -pool limitation that 
component-level tests did not, which the fallback ladder in the deployed system addresses. Four threats to validity 
remain. (i) Labels are catalogue-derived proxies, not human preferences. (i

6. Discussion 
6.1 Interpretation of the Compatibility Results 
The most informative result is a negative one. After rebalancing, the dual -path network reached 0.789 test 
accuracy but remained well below the linear model (0.932), and the validation sweep gave the linear model full 
weight. Three observations explain this. First, the labelled set is small: 948 training pairs cannot support a network 
with a six-figure parameter count, which is the memorisation-versus-generalisation trade-off that motivated wide-
and-deep models [9]. Second, the metadata -only model (0.928) is almost as accurate as the linear model with 
visual features (0.932), which suggests that the proxy labels depend mainly on category and colour. High accuracy 
therefore reflects, in part, the model recovering it

erefore reflects, in part, the model recovering its own labelling rule rather than independent knowledge of what 
people consider well matched. Third, the visual signal alone is informative (0.705) but weaker, so a deep visual 
branch has little to add until more or better labels are available. For this reason the accuracy figures should be 
read as evidence that the pipeline learns what the labels encode, not as evidence about shopper taste. 
6.2 Stability and Design Choices 
The weight-sensitivity analysis shows that the identity of the top five outfits depends on the balance between 
relevance and compatibility. The compatibility -led default (0.6 and 0.4) and the 0.55 compatibilit y floor are 
therefore stated design decisions, not optima; validating them requires human preference data

ma; validating them requires human preference data or implicit 
feedback such as clicks and cart additions. Following [12], the sensitivity is reported rather than hidden. Likewise, 
the reuse cap acts on product identifiers, so near-identical items under different identifiers can still repeat; a cap 
defined on embedding similarity is the natural next step. 
6.3 Trade-offs of Pre-Computation 
Pre-computing recommendations makes the application deterministic, fast and free to run, and it keeps price and 
stock live because they are joined at request time. The costs are three. The profile space is discrete: only body 
shape, size, occasion and season influence the outfits, so two shoppers with the same four valu es see the same 
five outfits, and finer measurements (for example a different

, and finer measurements (for example a different waist -to-hip ratio within the same shape) do not 
change the result. Products added to the catalogue are not ranked until the index is regenerated. And the season 
defaults to the current date, so the same profile yields different outfits across the year, which is intended but 
should be communicated to the shopper. Serving the model live from a separate free -tier host may be possible, 
but it was not adopted or tested in this project, because it would add a second runtime to maintain. 
6.4 Relation to Existing Work 
The engine shares its main ingredients with recent systems: fashion CLIP embeddings and occasion priors 
expressed as prompts [8], and ranking that discourages repetition [7] . It differs in treating body shape, size

7.1 Conclusion 
This work designed and built FitStyle AI, a low -cost web application that combines body measurement, outfit 
recommendation and virtual try-on in one shopping workflow. From a single full-body photograph and her height, 
the shopper receives a body shape and a clothing size, five complete outfits for her size, body shape, occasion and 
season, and a preview of the selected garments on her own photograph. Only the database, authent ication and
